correctness.rationale: For a unit direction \(p\), the tetrahedral frame coordinates \(t_i=p\cdot u_i\) satisfy exactly \(\sum t_i=0\) and \(\sum t_i^2=4/3\), and conversely parameterize the direction sphere. At fixed \(x=\rho/R>0\), the squared product is \(F=\prod_i(1+x^2-2xt_i)\). Away from the unique possible zero case \(x=1,t_i=1\), Lagrange multipliers for \(\log F\) force every \(t_i\) to satisfy one nonzero quadratic, so an extremum has two coordinate values. The two constraints leave only the \(1+3\), \(3+1\), and \(2+2\) symmetry types. Their exact values \(A,C,B\) obey \(A-C=-64x^3(x^2+x+1)/27<0\) and \(B-C=64x^3(x^2-x+1)/27>0\), hence \(A<C<B\) for every \(x>0\). Taking square roots gives the stated endpoints and equality rays; continuity on the connected sphere gives the full interval. The boundary cases \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) are handled explicitly.
risks: No computational experiment is used to justify an infinite step; floating-point checks only replay consequences of the analytic proof.

value.rationale: The product of distances to fixed vertices is a natural symmetric geometric invariant, with contemporary literature treating analogous product optimization in triangles. Fixing \(OP\) is the canonical rotation-invariant constraint for a regular tetrahedron. The theorem gives the complete sharp range for every radius, exact equality geometry, and a saddle branch ordering rather than a single inequality or isolated extremum. This is a natural classification of radial anisotropy of the tetrahedral distance product, not an arbitrary parameter slice or a recomputation of the known quartic relation.
risks: Value is specific to the three-dimensional regular case; no downstream higher-dimensional theorem is claimed.
